name: Sara Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. This is confidential. What fills an ordinary day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach beginner clarinet groups at the arts centre, play simple parts for a monthly recording session and prepare practice notes for families. I left school after secondary classes, and I still ask older players to show me tricky fingerings rather than pretending I know them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the work support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Jules works shifts at a care home, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My centre fee is high for junior music work, we have about ten months of expenses saved, and several similar centres are nearby.

say: I'd say **beginner playing** still takes a listening teacher and steady practice.
I'd accept **faster registers** while keeping the two paid group hours.
think: My **ten-month reserve** and summer contract protect the mortgage from one moved session.
Several nearby **centres** give me alternatives if next term changes.
do: Keep the **two clarinet groups** and monthly recording session through this year's contract.
Get a **paid-hour letter** before planning next term's mortgage payments.
feel: I feel **calm** because contracted teaching covers ordinary booking gaps.
S0.quote: A register can count a class; it cannot hear a clarinet squeak.
fieldNote: Her **high junior pay** and ten-month reserve make a mild scenario secure for the household.
She stays with **familiar teaching** and does not use AI even for routine work.

steps.text: Keep two clarinet groups and monthly studio sessions during contract
Get centre paid-hour letter before planning next term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the parents the centre can sort its registers faster, but the reed still squeaks until a child learns where to put a finger. My Monday and Wednesday groups are booked through summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I never use AI, and a little office automation would not change the paid group hours. We have ten months of expenses saved, my centre fee is good for a junior player, and there are several other centres nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the two beginner clarinet groups and the monthly recording session through this year's contract. Before accepting next term, I'll get the centre's paid-hour letter and show it to my partner Jules so our mortgage plan uses real dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few years in this picture. A moved recording session would be disappointing, but it would not threaten a mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when a recording date moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio moved a session in May and paid me in June. The centre fee covered that month, so I did not ask Jules to take an extra care-home shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a beginner who asks about an app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a new player to practise holding one steady note before worrying about an app. A child knows when a teacher is listening to the sound, not just ticking a box. A register can count a class; it cannot hear a clarinet squeak.

say: I'd ask for a written **paid-hours breakdown** before software changes the timetable.
I'd ask parents which **live lessons** they would still pay to attend.
think: **Arranging and feedback** hours are about a fifth of my centre fee and may shrink.
Our **reserve** buys search time, but a lower net fee could still hurt.
do: Request a **written breakdown** of teaching and preparation hours this term.
Apply in **first disruption year** if prep hours fall, junior vacancy opens, audition qualifies, pickup works and net pay replaces lost fees.
Keep **centre groups** while auditioning for any paid orchestra role.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a likely fifth of my pay shrinking.
S1.quote: Working faster does not make the centre pay me for the hour it removes.
fieldNote: She expects a **real income loss** from simple thinking tasks despite ten months saved.
Her **orchestra application** requires an actual vacancy, a feasible audition and family-compatible net pay.

steps.text: Request written centre teaching and arrangement hours
Apply first year if prep fees fall and orchestra vacancy fits audition, pickup and net pay
Keep centre groups while auditioning for paid role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre manager to say plainly which paid hours disappear when software handles bookings and practice checks. I would ask the parents what live playing they still value, instead of arguing about machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The simple arrangements and pupil feedback notes bring about a fifth of my centre fee. I expect those hours to shrink before a robot can play clarinet, and I won't make the same monthly amount just by working faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This term I'll ask for a written breakdown of group hours and arrangement hours. In the first year of this change, if the centre cuts a paid preparation block, I'll apply to a nearby children's orchestra for its posted junior rehearsal role only if the hours fit school pickup and the net fee replaces that block.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing part of my own pay, despite our reserve. Ten months saved gives me time to reject an offer that would leave the children waiting outside school. Working faster does not make the centre pay me for the hour it removes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the nearby orchestra role actually available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The orchestra advertised a junior role last year, but I do not know whether one will open. I would check the audition level before applying; I am still learning the harder passages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the centre for an audition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep teaching at the centre while I audition. If another group wants me for an unpaid trial, I'll ask what a paid rehearsal would look like instead.

say: I'd demand a written **2028 pay plan** before preparation hours change.
I'd keep **booked clarinet groups** while live teaching still pays.
think: **AGI in 2028** could remove simple arrangements before robot players arrive around 2031.
A lost **fifth of my fee** would matter, though ten months saved allow a search.
do: Get next year's **paid-hour plan** and list real centre openings this week.
Audition in the **first year after 2028** if preparation pay ends, only for open posts accepting my education and covering net losses.
Keep **existing groups** while a three-month audition budget protects the reserve.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost preparation pay, with savings for a measured search.
S2.quote: Ten months saved lets me search; it does not turn a lost paid hour into free time.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 thinking fees** from live playing exposed to 2031 robots.
Her **auditions** require actual openings, qualifying education, viable net pay and a capped savings budget.

steps.text: Request written centre paid-hour plan before 2028
Audition after 2028 if preparation pay ends and open qualifying post replaces lost net pay
Keep existing groups while limiting audition spending to three months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre that 2028 is too soon to quietly remove paid preparation hours. I would keep the clarinet classes running while parents and the centre still book them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could arrange simple parts, answer parents and give practice feedback cheaper than I can. Robots able to play hands-on music arrive around 2031, but a fifth of my fee could vanish first; ten months of savings and Jules's care-home wage make a search possible, not free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the manager for next year's paid-hour plan and list the centres that have advertised teaching posts. In the first year after 2028, if preparation pay ends, I'll audition for an open beginner-ensemble post only if it accepts my secondary education and the net fee after travel beats the lost hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing work I have only recently learned to do well. I can pay the mortgage while I search, but I do not want to spend a year of savings replacing a fifth of my wage. Ten months saved lets me search; it does not turn a lost paid hour into free time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your education qualify for those posts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One nearby centre usually asks for a diploma I do not have. I would not treat that listing as an option until they confirm my playing test can count instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much savings would you spend on auditions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules and I would set a three-month search budget before touching savings. If no suitable post appears, I would keep my existing group hours and stop applying to jobs that require credentials I cannot afford.

say: I'd ask for a **paid beginner ensemble** with loan instruments.
I'd keep **live group playing** at the centre while software changes practice work.
think: **AGI in 2031** could end arrangements before robot players arrive around 2034.
**Ordinary software** may erode preparation fees earlier, so the household pay can shrink.
do: Propose a **six-week ensemble** next spring only with signed pay, loan instruments, maintenance and six paid families.
Refund **families** if fewer than six pay and keep the two existing groups.
Run the **ensemble** in the first year after 2031 only if six renew and its fee covers hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** because preparation pay may fade before AGI arrives.
S3.quote: I won't buy six clarinets to find out whether six children want to play.
fieldNote: Her **six-family threshold** and centre-owned instruments keep the class from draining the reserve.
She requires **maintenance responsibility** as well as a signed fee before promising loan instruments.

steps.text: Propose centre ensemble only with six paid families, signed fee and maintained loan instruments
Refund families if fewer than six pay for ensemble
Run ensemble after 2031 only if six renew and fee covers hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell parents five years gives us time to build real group playing, not just better practice sheets. I would ask the centre for a paid beginner ensemble that children can join without buying instruments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could take arrangements and feedback notes, with robot players about 2034. I have time to strengthen my teaching, but those preparation fees may fade sooner under ordinary software, so our own income is still at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'll propose a six-week beginner ensemble only if the centre signs a teaching fee, lends instruments and six families pay for a full term. By 2031 I'll seek another term of the group; in the first year after AGI, I'll run it only if six families renew and the fee still covers my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about preparation fees fading before the five years are up. The savings mean I can stop a class that fails, but cannot pretend a lost centre fee never happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy instruments for the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre can lend its instruments for a first term if it agrees to keep them clean. If only four families pay, I would refund them and continue the two existing groups. I won't buy six clarinets to find out whether six children want to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would maintain the loan instruments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre would have to name who maintains and cleans loan instruments. I won't tell families the instruments are ready until the centre agrees to do that.

say: I'd ask schools for **paid music support** rather than a volunteer title.
I'd keep **junior tutors paid** while teaching children to play together.
think: At **53**, I still need work when AGI arrives in 2036.
**Early fee erosion** threatens income before robots reach live playing around 2039.
do: Ask **two schools** about support credentials and grant funding this year.
Enrol only if **grant, acceptance and childcare** gates are met before 2036.
Take a **posted school job** in the first year after 2036 only with written net pay covering mortgage and travel.
feel: I feel **anxious** because preparation fees can fade before 2036.
S4.quote: A course the schools won't accept is an expensive way to stay in the same job.
fieldNote: She treats **ten years** as time to qualify, not as proof that preparation fees remain safe.
A **written net offer** and childcare shift protect her household before any school transition.

steps.text: Ask two schools about music support credentials
Enrol before 2036 only if grant funds accepted course and childcare works
Take posted aide job first year after 2036 only if net offer covers mortgage and travel
Keep centre groups until school signs paid offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre that ten years is enough to help young players learn properly, provided we keep paying tutors. I would not ask a junior musician to work without a fee for the sake of a nice poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, with robot players around 2039. The preparation fees could fall well before then, so I need paid school work that can replace them; I am not close enough to retirement to simply wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask two schools what a classroom music support post requires and enrol in a course only if a grant covers fees, the schools accept its certificate and Jules can cover childcare. By 2036 I'll aim for six months' expenses untouched; in the first year after AGI, I'll take a school post only if advertised paid hours and a written net offer cover the mortgage and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the early erosion of preparation pay, though ten years allows more careful training. Our savings can cover a gap, but they should not pay for a course the schools won't accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the course fit the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger child still needs someone home after school. Jules would need an earlier care-home shift for the course days; if that is unavailable, I will wait for the next intake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you leave your centre groups?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the centre clarinet groups until a school signs a real offer. If nothing opens, the two groups and Jules's wage still cover the mortgage today. A course the schools won't accept is an expensive way to stay in the same job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the centre could remove paid preparation hours quickly, though we have savings for a search. A written pay plan and real openings that accept my education would help me choose another post without gambling the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who cleans the loan instruments between children's lessons. A free clarinet can cost families plenty if nobody is responsible for keeping it ready.

headlineQuote: A free clarinet can cost families plenty if nobody is responsible for keeping it ready.
portrait: Sara is a **43-year-old** junior clarinet teacher with secondary schooling, centre groups, monthly recording work and children at home.
Her **high junior fee**, ten-month reserve, Jules's wage and several nearby centres protect the mortgage from short gaps.
She avoids **AI tools** while expecting paid preparation and feedback tasks to shrink before robots reach playing three years later.
She requires **written pay**, accepted qualifications, childcare cover and real vacancies before moving to school work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because preparation pay could end quickly despite the household reserve.
whatWouldHelp: A **written pay plan** and nearby posts accepting her education would support a careful job search.
